idiom_name: PORO: reader methods over primitives, private helpers, freeze
implementation_notes: The Ruby idiom is the PORO (plain old Ruby object): a class in its own file that requires nothing from the rest of the model, exposes reader methods over primitives, and keeps helpers `private` so only the implicit receiver can call them; `freeze` in the constructor and hand-written `==`/`eql?`/`hash` turn it into a value. That replaces the classic private-members structure with file-level isolation plus visibility, and nothing in the class's own definition references another domain concept. Ruby enforces none of it (classes can be reopened anywhere), so the standalone quality lives in the file boundary and in review. For data-carrying values, `Data.define` (Ruby 3.2) removes the hand-written equality; a PORO remains right when behaviour dominates the data or older Rubies must be supported.
code_sketch:
# money.rb - imports nothing from the rest of the model
class Money
  attr_reader :minor, :currency
  def initialize(minor, currency)
    @minor, @currency = Integer(minor), normalise(currency).freeze
    freeze
  end
  def plus(other) = Money.new(minor + other.minor, currency)
  private
  def normalise(code) = code.to_s.upcase
end
pitfalls: Open classes: any file can reopen the class and add methods or model knowledge, so the boundary is a convention protected by review and linting, not a language guarantee.
`dup`, `clone` and `Marshal` bypass `freeze` and any validation performed in `initialize`, producing invalid copies if callers use them; override `initialize_copy` when invariants matter.
Hand-written value semantics are easy to get subtly wrong: `==` without `eql?`/`hash` breaks the class as a Hash key, which is exactly the bug `Data.define` removes.
Rails conventions re-couple POROs dropped into `app/models` (autoloading, an ActiveRecord base class); keep standalone classes in plain libraries or plain namespaces.

variants.name: Data.define value object
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby 3.2 added `Data.define(:minor, :currency)`: it declares the members, generates reader methods, value equality and `with`-based copies, accepts no writers, and freezes instances, so the type's meaning is exactly the declaration and it can be used as a Hash key immediately. Add a block to override `initialize` for validation or defaults. Use it for standalone values (Money, Percentage, identifiers, coordinates); keep the PORO when behaviour dominates the data, when partial/optional records are needed (all `Data` members are mandatory), or when Ruby < 3.2 must be supported.
variants.code_sketch:
Money = Data.define(:minor, :currency) do
  def initialize(minor:, currency:)
    super(minor: Integer(minor), currency: currency.to_s.upcase)
  end

  def plus(other) = with(minor: minor + other.minor)
end

Money.new(minor: 100, currency: "eur")   # => #<data Money minor=100, currency="EUR">
pitfalls: All members are mandatory (unlike `Struct`), so optional fields need a Null Object or a defaulted wrapper rather than a nil member.
Immutability is shallow: a mutable member object is shared between a value and its `with` copy, and `Data` performs no deep enforcement.
`Data` has no writers and is not enumerable, so code written against `Struct` (members, `each`, in-place updates) must switch APIs.
